chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Faddal from some of our companions from Amr ibn al-Yas' said:

I performed Hajj with my father while I was a young boy (sarurah), and I said: 'I would like to make my Hajj on behalf of my mother, for she has died.' He said: 'Let me ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) for you.' So al-Yas' said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) while I was listening: 'May I be your ransom, this son of mine is a sarurah and his mother has died, and he wishes to make his Hajj for her. Is that permissible for him?' Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'It is recorded for him and for her, and it is recorded for him the reward of the piety (al-barri).'

Because in this report it is not indicated that it exempts both of them simultaneously and removes the obligation (fard) from each one of them. The meaning in this hadith is that if the son intended by this Hajj to perform the Qada (make-up) for his mother, then it exempts her, and he remains obligated to perform the Hajj for himself from his own wealth, according to what we have previously mentioned from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Khalaf from Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him). And if he intended the Hajj for himself and for her together, then it exempts him, and she is entitled to the reward of the Hajj, although the obligation (fard) is not removed from her. And that which indicates this interpretation is what was narrated:

key_terms.صَرُورَةٌ: A young boy, typically before puberty or early childhood
key_terms.قَضَاءً: Make-up (performing an obligation after its time or for someone else)

ai.seo_question: Can a son perform Hajj for his deceased mother while he is still young, and does it count for both?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the dual nature of a son performing Hajj for his deceased mother while still young (*sarrur*), distinguishing between the legal discharge of the mother's obligation and the accumulation of reward for the son. The Imam explains that if the son intends it as *Qada* for her, her duty is fulfilled and he remains personally obligated for his own Hajj, receiving the reward of *al-barr* (piety); if he intends it for both, she receives the reward but her obligation is not necessarily discharged. This highlights the Shia juristic nuance that performing Hajj on behalf of another does not automatically exempt the performer from their own obligatory duty unless specified.
